headline: Training, contracts and a place in the trade
summary: Learning the trade, holding a license, joining a union and obtaining paid work were separate hurdles. These records show Black contractors, apprentices and union organizers changing access in specific places.
coverageNote: Five episodes across Chicago, New York and the Philadelphia area. Apprenticeship admission, contract requirements, union representation and an actual jobsite are kept separate.
question: Which apprenticeship record, union agreement or contractor project file connects this history to your work?

events.title: Sam Taylor creates a Black-owned electrical contractor
events.decisionMaker: Taylor founded and directed the Chicago business, with Stewart assisting him.
events.barrier: Racial exclusion restricted access to the trade and to full union membership.
events.change: After correspondence training and a Chicago electrician’s license, Taylor established Taylor Electric Company.
events.outcome: The company installed lights and doorbells and performed maintenance at Greer College.
events.limit: Business ownership did not itself secure full union membership; this account does not identify every employee.

source.title: IBEW · Black Leadership From Chicago’s South Side to the Sears Tower

events.title: Local 3 recruits beyond its traditional family route
events.people: Edward Mays, Harry Van Arsdale Jr. and the new apprentice class
events.decisionMaker: IBEW Local 3 broadened recruitment; a selection committee including Black electrician Edward Mays screened applicants.
events.barrier: The New York local had traditionally recruited apprentices through father–son relationships.
events.change: Recruitment letters reached civil-rights groups, employers and vocational schools, extending the pool of applicants.
events.outcome: A 1967 Labor Department study counted 240 Black apprentices among the 1,020 trainees admitted in 1962.
events.limit: Admission is documented; these figures do not prove that every trainee completed the program or secured continuing employment.

source.title: U.S. Department of Labor · Apprenticeship study (1967)
source.locator: Local 3 case study, printed pages 19–20; PDF pages 21–22

sources.title: Berkeley labor collection · Local 3 apprentice selection
sources.locator: The 1962 Apprentice Class of IBEW Local 3, printed pages 6–7

events.title: Arthur Fletcher attaches minority hiring goals to federal construction contracts
events.people: Arthur A. Fletcher and excluded minority construction workers
events.decisionMaker: Assistant Secretary of Labor Fletcher issued the Philadelphia Plan orders under Executive Order 11246.
events.barrier: The orders identified exclusionary union practices and contractors’ dependence on union hiring halls.
events.change: Bidders on covered contracts exceeding $500,000 in five Philadelphia-area counties had to commit to minority employment goals, including for electrical workers.
events.outcome: The Third Circuit upheld the plan in 1971 after contractors challenged its validity.
events.limit: A contracting requirement and a court ruling do not establish how many workers a particular contractor hired or retained.

source.title: Contractors Association of Eastern Pennsylvania v. Secretary of Labor, 442 F.2d 159
source.locator: Opening account of the June 27 and September 23, 1969 orders; concluding affirmance

events.title: Black and Hispanic electrical workers organize for union leadership
events.people: Leon Wilkerson, Johnny Walker and fellow minority IBEW delegates
events.decisionMaker: The delegates formed the Electrical Workers Minority Caucus and selected representatives to meet IBEW leaders.
events.barrier: Members challenged the limited representation of minorities on the union’s international staff.
events.change: Organizing at the Kansas City convention secured meetings with International President Charles Pillard and Treasurer Harry Van Arsdale Jr.
events.outcome: The caucus’s first executive committee met union leaders in September and November 1974, establishing an ongoing channel for advocacy.
events.limit: The organizational history documents representation and meetings; it does not quantify their effect on hiring or promotions.

source.title: Electrical Workers Minority Caucus · EWMC History
source.locator: Dorothy Fortier’s history, February 1, 2024; founding and 1974 meetings

events.title: Taylor Electric’s work reaches major Chicago stadiums
events.people: Rufus Taylor, Jessie Taylor Dinkins and Taylor Electric’s workers
events.decisionMaker: Taylor Electric’s leadership expanded the company into larger projects; the account does not identify the stadium contracting officials.
events.barrier: Owning a contracting business and obtaining large projects are distinct stages of access.
events.change: The Black-owned company moved from smaller commercial jobs into large construction and maintenance work.
events.outcome: IBEW records electrical maintenance at Comiskey Park and Soldier Field beginning in the early 1990s.
events.limit: The named contractor and jobsites are documented, but the crew, individual hiring decisions and a reader’s assignment remain unknown.

source.title: IBEW · Taylor Electric’s Chicago projects
source.locator: The Electrical Worker, February 2025, page 7; stadium maintenance paragraph
